title: The Inevitable Post About *That* Documentary
author: Educating Hat Beasts
summary: This Substack post, written by a home educator of disabled children and former community educator, dissects the fallout from a BBC Panorama documentary on Britain's Athena Learning Trust, a multi-academy chain whose harsh "no-excuses" behavioral regime allegedly pushed 500 of 6,000 pupils into home education. The author traces Athena's practices back to Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion playbook, arguing that techniques like uniform scripted phrases ("3-2-1 FOCUS") and reading rulers were applied rigidly across all students with no evidence base and no room for teacher judgment. Drawing on primary-teacher blogger Christopher Such's critique of reading-ruler research and on Pamela Hobart's data on the spread of ability within any classroom, the piece argues that treating thirty teenagers as functionally interchangeable inevitably fails a large minority, especially neurodivergent pupils. It closes by reframing the debate away from "is discipline good" toward how many students a public system can fail before its methods are questioned.
points: The author's central claim is that Athena's harm came not from having discipline but from applying one scripted behavioral technique uniformly to a student population where nearly half fall outside the instructional 'sweet spot' any single approach can reach.

Reading rulers, defended publicly as supporting dyslexic and SEND students, in fact have no direct evidence base, according to primary teacher-blogger Christopher Such, and can add rather than reduce cognitive load for students with motor or auditory processing differences.

Athena's suspension and home-education exodus rates suggest its celebrated exam-result gains may be partly explained by the departure of its most struggling students rather than by the pedagogy's effectiveness.

Staff testimony describing INSET training as 'indoctrination' and describing a culture where anyone 'could have worked off the street' and delivered the model points to a system prioritizing fidelity to technique over teacher judgment and experience.
quotes: It's the picture of Athena as an institution with little accountability to anyone; parents, staff or local councillors, wedded to an ideology of what education should look like. And not one that's left-right or traditional-progressive-coded either, but rather so wedded to the ideals of Doug Lemov's Teach Like A Champion that practitioners act(ed) almost like a cult.

Quite simply, if there is any research that directly explores whether it is beneficial for pupils to track text while listening to it being read aloud, then I haven't seen it. And it is certainly the case that classroom management strategies to facilitate this, such as the use of reading rulers, have also not been studied.

One of the most academically capable (and generally delightful) pupils I ever worked with had extreme difficulties with hand-eye coordination. Moving a ruler down a text as it was read to him was genuinely such a struggle that it would have distracted him from engaging with the text had I forced him to do so.

Pamela Hobart in Above Grade Level, for example, estimates that possibly 35% of students are one grade level above their classmates in reading or maths. Whereas perhaps as many as 13% are working three years behind.

According to government figures, the suspension rate at one trust school, Camborne Science and International Academy, reached the second-highest total in England in 2023/2024 and at Launceston was reportedly three times the national average.
It's more: how many young people need to leave a public institution 'for all' before we acknowledge it's not doing its job?
